newsitem.title: POLAND: NATO-Russia deal dispels some doubts, Rybkin says.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia deal dispels some doubts, Rybkin says.

text.p: The proposed NATO-Russia treaty is a well-prepared compromise which dispels some but not all of Moscow's doubts over the Western alliance's expansion, Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's Security Council, said on Monday.

"The NATO-Russia treaty removes a whole range of anxieties in Russia -- many but not all. It is the result of a compromise well-aimed, thought-through and worked out," Rybkin said after giving a lecture at Warsaw's Eastern Studies Centre think-tank.
"I want to believe that at the end of May the treaty between NATO and Russia will definitely be signed," he said.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin said last week he hoped the treaty could be signed on May 27.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said in Prague on Monday that this date was possible but Russia would continue to oppose the expansion of NATO, which plans at its Madrid summit in July to invite new members to begin entry negotiations.

These are expected to include Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary, all former Soviet satellite states. Moscow has said it views their membership of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as a threat to its security.
NATO and Russia are to hold a new round of talks on May 6 to try to overcome remaining Russian objections.

Such objections have been partly addressed by establishing a permanent consultative mechanism between Moscow and the alliance and by declaring that NATO has no intention of stationing nuclear arms or foreign troops in new member states.
Russia insists that new NATO members should not be allowed to improve their existing military infrastructureto bring it up to the pact's standards, a demand that NATO has refused.

Rybkin said that after long, hard talks there was now an understanding that Russia's fears had to be taken account of. Last month's Helsinki summit between Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin was part of this realisation, he said.
A reporter asked why Russia would sign the charter if, as Chernomyrdin said, the document did not fully satisfy it.
"Happily the Bolsheviks no longer hold power in Russia, as they used to solve problems along the principle: "everything, right away."
"I speak of the NATO-Russia agreement as a reasonable compromise which can be accepted at a specific moment under specific circumstances," Rybkin said.

Rybkin, who is on a two-day working visit to Poland, earlier held talks with Polish officials including his counterpart Marek Siwiec, chief of the presidential Bureau of National Security, and was due to meet President Aleksander Kwasniewski on Tuesday.
